reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Remember the classic six P's: pruritic, purple (violaceous), polygonal, planar (flat-topped) papules and plaques
Lesions favour the flexor wrists, forearms, and ankles, and fine white lacy lines on the surface (Wickham striae) are a helpful diagnostic clue
New lesions can appear along lines of trauma or scratching (Koebner phenomenon)
Oral lichen planus commonly presents as a white reticular lacy pattern on the buccal mucosa; erosive oral or genital disease is painful and warrants monitoring
Nail involvement can cause ridging and, if severe, scarring with pterygium formation, while scalp disease (lichen planopilaris) causes scarring alopecia
Consider a lichenoid drug eruption when a similar rash follows introduction of a new medication, and screen for hepatitis C where locally relevant
Treatment centres on topical corticosteroids for cutaneous and localised mucosal disease, with phototherapy or systemic immunomodulators for widespread or resistant cases
Long-standing erosive oral or genital lichen planus carries a small risk of malignant transformation and should be followed up
reference.pathophysiology: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated inflammatory disorder in which cytotoxic CD8 T lymphocytes target basal keratinocytes, apparently in response to an altered self-antigen. The resulting band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction produces the characteristic histological features of basal cell degeneration, a saw-tooth epidermal profile, hypergranulosis, and apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte bodies). Pigment released from damaged basal cells accounts for the post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation often seen, particularly in darker skin. Triggers can include certain drugs (lichenoid reactions) and, in some populations, hepatitis C infection.
additionalDifferentials: Discoid lupus erythematosus (for scalp and mucosal disease)
Leukoplakia or candidiasis for oral white lesions
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing a lichenoid interface dermatitis in uncertain cases
Direct immunofluorescence to help distinguish from lupus or immunobullous disease when needed
Hepatitis C testing where epidemiologically appropriate
Review of medication history to identify a lichenoid drug trigger
Biopsy of persistent erosive or indurated oral or genital lesions to exclude dysplasia or malignancy
redFlags: Erosive oral or genital disease with non-healing or indurated areas suggesting malignant change
Scarring alopecia or nail destruction indicating a need for prompt treatment to limit permanent damage
Rapidly extensive eruption suggesting a drug cause requiring medication review
Severe painful mucosal disease impairing eating or causing significant morbidity
reference.prognosis: Cutaneous lichen planus is often self-limiting, frequently resolving within one to two years but leaving post-inflammatory pigmentation; mucosal, nail, and scalp forms tend to be chronic, and erosive mucosal disease requires long-term surveillance for malignant transformation.
pitfalls: Overlooking a lichenoid drug reaction and continuing the causative medication
Failing to examine the mouth, genitalia, nails, and scalp for additional sites of involvement
Not monitoring erosive oral or genital disease for malignant change
Attributing scarring alopecia to non-scarring causes and delaying treatment
management: Prescribe potent topical corticosteroids as first-line treatment for cutaneous lesions, with antihistamines for pruritus
Use topical calcineurin inhibitors or corticosteroid gels and mouthwashes for oral and genital erosive disease
Offer phototherapy (narrowband UVB or PUVA) for widespread cutaneous involvement
Reserve systemic therapy — corticosteroids, acitretin, ciclosporin, methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil — for severe or refractory disease
Review medications and withdraw a suspected lichenoid drug trigger, and screen for and treat hepatitis C where epidemiologically relevant
Maintain long-term surveillance of erosive oral and genital disease, with biopsy of persistent or indurated lesions to exclude malignant transformation
Refer nail and scalp (lichen planopilaris) involvement early to limit permanent scarring
